newsitem.title: UK: Bunker traders warned to check credit ratings.
newsitem.headline: Bunker traders warned to check credit ratings.

text.p: Bunker traders, suppliers, shipowners and charterers have been warned to take more care in checking credit ratings of those involved in chain bunker deals.

Speaking at a Bunker News European Convention in London, SPET liquidator Mark Chapple, a senior insolvency specialist with Baker & McKenzie, said there were a number of lessons to be learned from the collapse of Australian bunker traders SPET (South Pacific Energy Trading) and William Scollay & Co Ltd of New Zealand in 1996.
SPET had amassed deficits of $16 million when it went into liquidation.
Chapple said credit checking was inadequate during the SPET/Scollay affair. "No one appeared to be phased by the fact that SPET had paid up capital of only two Australian dollars."
He added that too many traders and operators were blinded by the discounts SPET was giving and dropped established contracts where there was less risk.
Ince & Co partner Jonathan Lux said it was important to sign contracts with known and reputable brokers.
Lux added: "Require of brokers that they will not introduce further traders into the deal or that they have unencumbered title to the bunkers when they are passed on."
Jeanne Kostiuk of Tomen America, Inc said, "Credit departments need to talk to each other to know who we are dealing with in order to protect ourselves and prevent this happening again."

Chapple said that in January 1995, SPET owner Martin Lawson started a trade involving a monthly $1 million transaction to supply bunkers for the owners and operators of a vessel named the Rangitoto. SPET claimed the physical supplier was Caltex Oil (NZ) Ltd.

"Subsequent investigations were to uncover that Caltex NZ did not supply any fuel to the vessel, or know anything else about the alleged transactions, and that the Rangitoto was not capable of taking anywhere near 5,000 metric tonnes of fuel."
"Martin Lawson was to subsequently concede in his public examinations that at least he knew that what purported to be legitimate and regular trading transactions were in fact shams," Chapple said.
